READING

**The capital comparison**

TARNSIDE costs £1,730,000. VELLACOTT costs £2,680,000 net (after the Brindlemere sale). The difference is £950,000 more for VELLACOTT upfront. That is the number everything else has to be tested against.

**The fuel saving does the heavy lifting**

VELLACOTT saves £190,000 a year in fuel relative to TARNSIDE. At that rate, the £950,000 gap is closed in exactly five years. Every year after year five, VELLACOTT is £190,000 ahead in cash terms, permanently, before any other difference is counted. Cormorant Sound Ferries holds a year-round licence. The vessel is not going away. A five-year payback on a marine asset is well within normal planning horizons, and the savings compound indefinitely thereafter.

**The hull age matters more than the engines**

Under TARNSIDE you spend £1,730,000 and end up with a 1995 hull that carries rebuilt engines. The hull was clean in March 2026, but the surveyor only speaks to today. A 32-year-old steel hull in a tidal, Scottish-waters operation will require steelwork eventually; the only question is when and how much. No figure for future hull intervention appears in the TARNSIDE case, which means the £1,730,000 almost certainly understates the true ten-year cost of that course. Under VELLACOTT you hold a 2017 hull that should have decades of useful life ahead with no equivalent exposure.

**The twelve-week yard period is a real cost and a real risk**

TARNSIDE includes £310,000 for a charter cover that is agreed only "in principle." A charter in principle is not a charter in hand. If that arrangement falls through or proves inadequate, there is no fallback except a twelve-week gap in service on a licensed route. Twelve weeks in the yard in winter also introduces schedule risk — weather delays, parts delays, subcontracted labour — that could extend into the May peak. VELLACOTT has no yard period at all. The Suilvenaig is available for handover on 2026-11-20, which is before the Brindlemere re-engining even begins.

**The masters question is solvable**

Losing two masters from nine to get to seven is a genuine reduction in roster depth, and scheduling seven people through a six-week endorsement course without leaving the vessel uncovered requires careful planning. But it is a one-time administrative problem, not a structural one. The courses can be staggered: send two masters now (one from the seven who are willing, plus a second), have two endorsed by handover date, then pipeline the remaining five over the following months while the newly-endorsed masters crew the Suilvenaig. If the roster feels tight at seven, one targeted recruitment replaces what was lost. There is no equivalent fix for a 1995 hull.

**The insurance gap needs closing, but is not a blocker**

The broker has not yet quoted on the Suilvenaig. This is an open item and should be resolved before any contract is signed. However, the direction of travel is not alarming: a 2017-built vessel is, all else equal, a better insurance risk than a thirty-one-year-old one. The TARNSIDE advantage here — known terms on the Brindlemere — is real but is really just the insurance company's familiarity with an old ship. The more likely outcome is that the Suilvenaig quote comes in at comparable or marginally worse rates, not that it is refused or priced at a level that inverts the economics. Ingrid should obtain that quote immediately, before any letter of intent on the Suilvenaig, and treat it as a condition of proceeding.

**The Brindlemere sale window**

Kittiwake's £610,000 valuation holds until 2027-02-11. Suilvenaig handover is 2026-11-20. That gives roughly twelve weeks to move the Brindlemere. Twelve weeks to sell a surveyed, running ferry on the open market with a motivated seller is tight but workable, especially given Hebridean & Vaile's long relationship with the vessel and knowledge of the potential buyer pool. The VELLACOTT calculation only works if that sale completes at or near £610,000; Ingrid should begin marketing now, in parallel with due diligence on the Suilvenaig, and should not allow a gap between acquisition and disposal that carries both vessels simultaneously for longer than the cash position supports.

**Summary of the balance**

| Factor | TARNSIDE | VELLACOTT |
|---|---|---|
| Net capital outlay | £1,730,000 | £2,680,000 |
| Annual fuel gap | −£190,000 worse | Baseline |
| Break-even horizon | — | ~5 years |
| Hull risk | High and rising | Low for 15+ years |
| Yard disruption | 12 weeks + charter risk | None |
| Masters | All nine retained | Seven retained; training required |
| Insurance | Known | Unknown — must obtain quote |
| Long-term economics | Deteriorating | Improving |

The insurance question is the only point where TARNSIDE holds a clear and unresolved advantage, and that advantage is almost certainly temporary. Every other factor, weighted over a reasonable planning horizon, favours VELLACOTT.

---

READING
  VELLACOTT costs £950,000 more upfront but saves £190,000 a year in fuel, paying back in five years, while delivering a 2017 hull in place of a 1995 one; the masters and insurance complications are manageable one-time problems, whereas the Brindlemere's aging hull is a structural and escalating liability. The instruction is to get the broker's Suilvenaig quote before signing anything, and to begin marketing the Brindlemere immediately.

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The £950,000 additional capital cost of VELLACOTT is recovered through fuel savings alone within five years, after which the operation is permanently better-off while holding a vessel with twenty-two more years of hull life and none of the escalating structural risk that a 1995 ship will inevitably carry.
